canonicalStatement: Let f(n) -> infinity (possibly very slowly). Is there a graph of infinite chromatic number such that every finite subgraph on n vertices can be made bipartite by deleting at most f(n) edges?
closeReason: NEITHER branch of the contract is met. Branch A (affirmative) requires a graph of infinite chromatic number for EVERY f -> infinity; nothing here constructs any such graph. Branch B (negative) requires exhibiting an f -> infinity for which no such graph exists; nothing here does that either. What is proved is the rate-free half only: infinite chromatic number FORCES the bipartite-defect function to be unbounded, with no rate. The entire open content of Erdos 74 is the rate, so this is progress toward well-posedness, not toward closure.

novelty.reason: The bound chi(G) <= 2^(B+1) from a bounded bipartite-defect is elementary and folklore: a graph B edges away from bipartite has chromatic number bounded in terms of B, plus de Bruijn-Erdos compactness. The sharp classical bound is chi <= 1 + sqrt(1+8B), better than the 2^(B+1) proved here. NO CLAIM OF MATHEMATICAL NOVELTY IS MADE.
novelty.whatIsNew: The FORMALIZATION is new. The formal-conjectures file FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/74.lean carries only two `category test` lemmas (nonempty, bddAbove) and two `sorry`d research statements. It proves nothing about the defect function. The 16 sorry-free theorems banked here are the first machine-checked content about those objects, including a calibration theorem and a load-bearing-guard audit finding.

literatureState.knownPositive: Rodl: there is such a graph (chromatic number aleph_0) for f(n) = eps*n, any fixed eps > 0. Also proved for hypergraphs.
literatureState.knownNegative: Fails (even for f(n) >> n) if the graph has chromatic number aleph_1 [Erdos-Hajnal-Szemeredi, EHS82; Komjath, arXiv math/0212064].
literatureState.gapThisCampaignDidNotTouch: Everything between bounded f and eps*n. The result banked here sits at the trivial end of that gap.
literatureState.sourceOfLiteratureFacts: erdosproblems.com/74 via web search 2026-09-05; the site itself returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so these attributions are SECOND-HAND and should be re-verified against EHS82 and Rodl 1982 before any outward use.

results.name: colorable_of_bounded_defect
results.statement: For G : SimpleGraph V and B : Nat, if (forall n, maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite G n <= B) then G.Colorable (2^(B+1)).
results.note: Main theorem. Finite-set induction removing one deleted edge at a time (each reinstated edge at most doubles the palette), then Mathlib's de Bruijn-Erdos compactness SimpleGraph.nonempty_hom_of_forall_finite_subgraph_hom.

results.name: exists_defect_gt_of_chromaticNumber_top
results.statement: If G.chromaticNumber = top then for every B there is an n with B < maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite G n.
results.note: The rate-free half of Erdos 74: infinite chromatic number forces the defect function to be unbounded. It gives NO rate, and the open problem is entirely about the rate.

results.name: no_graph_for_bounded_f
results.statement: For bounded f there is NO graph of infinite chromatic number whose n-vertex subgraphs are all within f n edges of bipartite.
results.note: So the answer to the Erdos 74 question is unconditionally NO for every bounded f. This is a genuine negative answer to a degenerate sub-case, NOT to the problem, whose hypothesis is f -> infinity.

results.name: erdos74_hypothesis_sharp
results.statement: A monotone f : Nat -> Nat that does not tend to infinity is bounded, hence admits no witness graph.
results.note: Shows the `Tendsto f atTop atTop` hypothesis in the formal-conjectures statement of erdos_74 is NECESSARY and cannot be dropped.

results.name: minEdgeDistToBipartite_eq_zero_iff
results.statement: For A with A.verts.Finite: minEdgeDistToBipartite A = 0 iff A.coe is bipartite.
results.note: CALIBRATION. Proves the defect function is not degenerate on the domain the problem uses. Without this, a theorem about a secretly-zero function would prove nothing.

results.name: ncard_hazard_infinite_edgeSet
results.statement: The complete graph on Nat, as a subgraph of itself, is NOT bipartite yet has minEdgeDistToBipartite = 0.
results.note: AUDIT FINDING. Set.ncard of an infinite set is 0, so deleting an infinite edge set reports cost 0. Consequence: the `A.verts.Finite` guard inside subgraphEdgeDistsToBipartite is LOAD-BEARING. The formal-conjectures file does carry that guard, so its statement is SOUND; this records why the guard can never be removed. No defect is claimed against that file.

checks: IsBipartite resolves to Mathlib SimpleGraph.IsBipartite := G.Colorable 2. Correct.
G.chromaticNumber = top in Nat-infinity means not finitely colourable, i.e. infinite chromatic number in the intended sense. Correct for the existential branch.

maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite ranges over ARBITRARY Subgraph G, while its docstring says `induced`. Benign: min-defect is monotone under adding edges, so the supremum is attained at induced subgraphs and the two readings agree.
Set.ncard-of-infinite-set collapse is real but GUARDED by A.verts.Finite; proved as ncard_hazard_infinite_edgeSet.
sSup over Nat returns junk 0 on unbounded sets, but BddAbove is proved in the source file, so maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite is meaningful.
For finite V the set subgraphEdgeDistsToBipartite G n is empty for n > card V, so sSup = 0 there. Harmless: the statement is existential over V and is witnessed on infinite V.

unprovedClaims: All literature attributions in `literatureState` are UNPROVED by this campaign and are second-hand (erdosproblems.com returned HTTP 403; facts came from web search summaries). They are recorded as context, not as results.
The exponent 2^(B+1) is not claimed optimal; the classical sharp bound is 1 + sqrt(1+8B) and is NOT formalized here.
nextMoves: Sharpen colorable_of_defect from 2^(B+1) to the classical 1 + sqrt(1+8B) by formalizing `a graph with chromatic number c has at least C(c,2) edges` plus the product-colouring chi(G) <= 2*chi(deleted-edge graph). Purely quantitative; does not approach the open problem.

The only routes that touch the real problem are (a) formalizing Rodl's f(n) = eps*n construction, which would give the first non-trivial POSITIVE instance in Lean, and (b) formalizing the aleph_1 negative theorem of EHS82. Both are substantial and both are published, so neither carries novelty.
